questions.stem: State the reactivity trend of Group 1 down the group.
questions.modelAnswer: The reactivity of Group 1 metals increases down the group.

questions.stem: Quote the calcium water-reaction description.
questions.modelAnswer: Calcium's reaction with cold water is fairly vigorous and exothermic.

questions.stem: Explain why the same argument covers both groups.
questions.modelAnswer: Both groups react by donating outer electrons, so whatever lowers the cost of that donation - growing radius and shielding - raises reactivity identically in both families.

questions.stem: If each added shell roughly halves the attraction the outer electron feels, estimate the attraction at the third element down relative to the first.
questions.modelAnswer: Two halvings leave one quarter of the original attraction, which is why the third element reacts so much more readily.

questions.stem: State what coats an alkali metal surface exposed to air.
questions.modelAnswer: A dull coating of the metal oxide covers the surface, which is the tarnish.

questions.stem: Write the general equation for a Group 1 metal with chlorine.
questions.modelAnswer: 2M (s) + Cl2 (g) -> 2MCl (s), a white solid in each case.

questions.stem: Explain why tarnishing accelerates down the group.
questions.modelAnswer: Tarnishing is oxidation by air, so the same falling ionisation cost that quicken the water reactions also speeds oxygen capture at the surface.

questions.stem: Sodium burns in chlorine with an intense orange flame. If 2.3 g of sodium (1 mole of atoms per 23 g) reacts fully, how many moles of Cl2 does it consume?
questions.modelAnswer: The equation 2Na + Cl2 -> 2NaCl pairs 2 Na atoms with 1 Cl2, so 1 mole of sodium atoms consumes 0.5 moles of chlorine molecules.

questions.stem: Write the general cold-water equation for Group 2 metals.
questions.modelAnswer: M (s) + 2H2O (l) -> M(OH)2 (s or aq) + H2 (g), except for beryllium.

questions.stem: State the peroxide footnote of the oxygen reactions.
questions.modelAnswer: Strontium and barium also form the peroxides SrO2 and BaO2 alongside their oxides.

questions.stem: Explain why steam enables magnesium's vigorous reaction while cold water does not.
questions.modelAnswer: Steam carries far more thermal energy and contacts the metal as a gas, so the surface oxide barrier breaks and the MgO + H2 reaction runs vigorously where cold water's slow attack never gets started.

questions.stem: Calcium reacts per Ca + 2H2O -> Ca(OH)2 + H2. How many moles of hydrogen form from 2 moles of calcium?
questions.modelAnswer: The 1:1 metal-to-hydrogen ratio gives 2 moles of H2 from 2 moles of calcium.
